title: Module 12 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A correlation of zero means the scatterplot shows no pattern at all.
items.why: A clear curved pattern can have r near zero.

items.s: One extreme point can create a strong correlation that the rest of the data do not show.
items.why: Always plot the data and consider the influence of outliers.

items.s: Studying only top-scoring students gives an accurate estimate of the correlation in the full population.
items.why: Range restriction shrinks the observed correlation.

items.s: If r is high within each of two groups, it will be high when the groups are pooled.
items.why: Pooling can raise, lower, or even reverse the correlation depending on how the groups differ on both variables.

items.s: Correlations are bounded between negative one and positive one.
items.why: Values outside the range indicate a calculation error.

items.s: A correlation of .30 is twice as strong as a correlation of .15 in terms of shared variance.
items.why: Shared variance is r squared. .09 versus .0225 is four times as much.

items.s: Unreliable measures can hide a real relationship.
items.why: Measurement error attenuates the observed correlation.

items.s: Seeing the scatterplot is optional once you have computed r.
items.why: Different patterns can produce the same r, so always look at the plot.
